item.title: An Unconditional Space-Approximation Lower Bound for Semi-Streaming Matching
item.description: arXiv:2610.36577v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove the first unconditional lower bound tradeoff between the number of passes and the approximation factor of maximum matchings in the semi-streaming model. Specifically, we show that any algorithm that outputs an $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation to maximum matching requires $\Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ passes for constant $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. Prior to our result, such tradeoffs were proven only conditioned on a certain combinatorial assumption about the density of Ruzsa-Szemer\'edi graphs. The state-of-the-art unconditional lower bound rules out any approximation factor better than $(8/9)$ in two passes but leaves open the possibility of a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation for any $\varepsilon > 0$ even in three passes. We provide two different proofs of our result: the first proof uses the recent hierarchical-embedding framework of Assadi, Konrad, Naidu, and Sundaresan (STOC 2024) along with combinatorial constructions using Ruzsa-Szemer\'edi graphs. The second extends the two-level Ruzsa-Szemer\'edi hierarchy of Konrad and Naidu (SODA 2024) beyond two levels and proves the corresponding communication lower bound directly by induction, rather than through a reduction to Index.
item.dc:creator: Yang P. Liu, Kheeran Naidu, Hoai-An Nguyen, Janani Sundaresan

item.title: Uniformity Testing for the Monomer-Dimer Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.36630v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study uniformity testing for the monomer-dimer model on a known graph $G=(V,E)$. Given samples from an unknown distribution $D_w(M)\propto \prod_{e\in M} w_e$ over matchings $M$ of $G$, we ask whether $D_w$ is the uniform distribution over all matchings of $G$ or is $\varepsilon$-far from it in total variation distance. Our main result is that, for every maximum-degree bound $\Delta$, uniformity can be tested with $\widetilde O_\Delta(\sqrt m/\varepsilon^2)$ samples, where $m=|E|$. We complement this with an information-theoretic lower bound for general graphs: for every pair of parameters $n\le m\le n^2$, there are graphs with $\Theta(n)$ vertices and $\Theta(m)$ edges on which every tester requires $\Omega(\sqrt m/\varepsilon^2)$ samples. Thus, for bounded-degree graph families with $m=\Theta(n)$, testing uniformity over the space of matchings has $\widetilde \Theta(\sqrt n/\varepsilon^2)$ sample complexity, in contrast with the $\Theta(n/\varepsilon^2)$ samples needed to estimate $D_w$ in total variation distance.
item.dc:creator: Joy Qiping Yang, Yuichi Yoshida

item.title: Differentially Private Preconditioned Power Iteration Method for Principal Component Analysis that Adapts to the Coherence
item.description: arXiv:2610.36691v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Principal Component Analysis (PCA), we are given as input a matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ and an integer $k\leq d$, and the goal is to find the top $k$ right-singular vectors of $A$. We consider the setting where each row of $A$ is the private data of an individual, and we design an $(\epsilon,\delta)$-differentially private algorithm whose utility guarantee improves with the coherence of the input matrix. Prior works were either restricted to the case $k=1$ or ensured significantly weaker privacy protections. Our algorithm is based on a preconditioned variant of the power iteration method that is designed to significantly reduce the noise needed to ensure privacy.
item.dc:creator: Duy V. Le, Ta Duy Nguyen, Alina Ene, Huy L. Nguyen

item.title: Linear-Time FPT Rectilinear Planarity Testing of Series-Parallel Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.37018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A planar graph is rectilinear planar if it admits a planar orthogonal drawing without bends. For series-parallel graphs in the variable embedding setting the best known testing algorithm takes $O(n^2)$ time. We show that rectilinear planarity of a series-parallel graph with maximum degree four can be tested in $2^{O(k)}\cdot n$ time, where $k$ is the number of degree-4 vertices; the planar embedding is not fixed. In particular, the running time is subquadratic when $k=o(\log n)$. Each node of the SPQ$^*$-tree stores the set of its admissible spiralities; we show that this set is a union of $2^{O(k)}$ arithmetic progressions of step two. All proofs are in the paper and are additionally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib.
item.dc:creator: Giacomo Ortali

item.title: Polynomial-Time Solvability of the Mixed Evacuation Problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.37065v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The mixed evacuation problem is a variant of the dynamic transshipment problem where there exist two modes of transportation and we allocate supplies to each mode of transportation in such a way that we can send all the supplies from sources to sinks within a given time limit. It is known that this problem can be solved in polynomial time when the number of sources and sinks is small. In this paper, we prove that the mixed evacuation problem can be solved in polynomial time with the ellipsoid method.
item.dc:creator: Naoyuki Kamiyama

item.title: Tight Bounds for Randomized Generalized $k$-Server on Uniform Metrics
item.description: arXiv:2610.37192v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the generalized $k$-server problem, each of $k$ servers moves in its own metric space, and a request $(r_1,\dots,r_k)$ is served once some server $i$ stands at the point $r_i$ of its space. We determine the randomized competitive ratio against an oblivious adversary when every space is a uniform metric. With unit distances the ratio is $\Theta(k\log k)$: we give a $(k+1)\ln(2k)$-competitive algorithm and show that for large $k$ every algorithm has ratio at least $\frac{1}{20}k\ln k$, improving the bounds $O(k^2\log k)$ and $\Omega(k)$ of Bienkowski, Je\.z, and Schmidt. When server $i$ pays $w_i$ per move, the ratio is $\exp(\Theta(k))$: we give a $20^k$-competitive algorithm, which also applies to weighted $k$-server on uniform metrics. This improves the $\exp(O(k^2))$ bound of Bijoy, Mondal, and Chiplunkar and matches the $\Omega(2^k)$ lower bound of Ayyadevara and Chiplunkar up to the base of the exponent. Both algorithms follow normalized weights exactly, through couplings whose expected movement is controlled by the decrease of the logarithm of the total weight. The lower bound hides a random permutation among the solutions of random permutation constraints, which split into small, well-separated components, and then forbids one position to one server at a time.
item.dc:creator: Junho Hwang

item.title: A Linear Kernel for Planar Semitotal Domination
item.description: arXiv:2610.37295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A set of vertices $S$ in a graph $G$ is a semitotal dominating set if $S$ is a dominating set and every vertex in $S$ has a witness, that is, another vertex in $S$ within distance at most two. The Semitotal Domination problem asks whether $G$ admits such a set of size at most $k$. We study this problem parameterized by the solution size. We provide a linear kernel of size $358k$ on planar graphs, a result that adds to several existing linear kernels for other domination variants on planar graphs. Additionally, we show Semitotal Domination is $W[2]$-hard on split graphs, on bipartite graphs and on $t$-claw-free graphs, it is $W[1]$-hard on circle graphs.
item.dc:creator: Paloma T. de Lima, Lukas Retschmeier

item.title: Online Interval Selection with Binary Predictions: Optimal Consistency and a Continuous Robustness Tradeoff
item.description: arXiv:2610.37361v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study online interval selection with binary predictions of membership in a final optimal solution. Requests arrive in arbitrary order; accepted requests may be revoked, but rejected or revoked requests cannot be recovered. With rewards proportional to interval length, the best consistency under finite strict robustness is $d=(3+\sqrt5)/2$ when both guarantees hold almost surely on each fixed input, including for randomized algorithms. A continuous lower bound forces consistency strictly above $d$ at every robustness budget below $4\varphi+3\approx9.472$, whereas our deterministic algorithm attains $d$ with exact robustness $\varphi^5\approx11.090$, where $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$. Each held interval inherits a ledger recording positive prediction mass lost through irrevocable decisions. A tunable replacement cost gives a continuous family with exact consistency throughout and exact robustness on two parameter intervals, including $(C,R)=(25/9,10)$ and $(4,7)$. Randomization permits expected consistency approaching one with finite expected robustness, whereas almost-sure robustness forces expected consistency strictly above two at every finite budget.
item.dc:creator: Zhong Han

item.title: Approximate Counting for Mixed $p$-Spin Glasses in Weak External Fields via Cluster Expansion
item.description: arXiv:2610.37630v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give algorithms for approximating the partition function $Z_N$ of the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick (SK) model and finite mixed Ising $p$-spin models with $p\ge 3$. The algorithms apply at a fixed margin below the second-moment threshold $\beta_{\mathrm f}$ with homogeneous weak external fields $|h|\leq\rho_0N^{-1/4}$, for fixed $\rho_0>0$. For any accuracy $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and failure parameter $\delta\in(0,1)$, they approximate $\log Z_N$ to additive error $\varepsilon$. The number of exact operations is polynomial jointly in $N$, $\varepsilon^{-1}$, and $\delta^{-1}$. The disorder variables have i.i.d symmetric distribution with unit variance. The failure probability is at most $\delta$ plus an explicit disorder tail bound. This tail bound tends to zero under a finite fourth moment condition. Our approach builds on the cluster expansions of Aizenman--Lebowitz--Ruelle~\cite{ALR87} and Dey--Wu~\cites{DW23,DW26}. For higher-order mixtures, we retain hypergraphs using few vertices and evaluate their total weight deterministically through local spin averages and inclusion--exclusion. For SK, we impose cutoffs on the number of vertices of degree at least three and on the total number of edges. We estimate the retained sum using randomized color coding~\cite{AYZ95}. A lower tail control based on reverse hypercontractivity~\cite{MOS13} converts the mean-square approximation of the normalized partition function into logarithmic accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Qiang Wu

item.title: Interactive Particle Systems on Hypergraphs, Drift Analysis and the WalkSAT algorithm
item.description: arXiv:1909.12353v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We analyze the expected running time of WalkSAT, a well-known local search procedure for satisfiability solving, on satisfiable instances of the k-XOR SAT problem. We obtain estimates of this expected running time by reducing the problem to a setting amenable to classical techniques from drift analysis. A crucial ingredient of this reduction is the definition of (new, explosive) hypergraph versions of interacting particle systems, notably of coalescing and annihilating random walks as well as the voter model. The use of these tools allows to show that the expected running time of WalkSAT depends on structural parameter (we call odd Cheeger drift) of the dual of the formula hypergraph.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Istrate, Cosmin Bonchis, Mircea Marin

item.title: Single-Range-Cover Search on DAGs: Average-Case Analysis, Efficient Implementations, Privacy Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2602.06860v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Extracting exact and complete information using range queries is not only time-inefficient, on average, but also susceptible to privacy breaches. As a remedy, Demertzis et al.~\cite{demertzis2016practical} (SIGMOD'16) introduced, in the context of searchable symmetric encryption, the principle of covering a query with a single canonical range using a DAG structure (TDAG). It was later formalized by Falzon et al.~\cite{falzon2022range} (VLDB'22) as the single range cover (SRC) search algorithm -- a faster and potentially privacy-preserving search principle. SRC-search can, however, produce false positives. In this work we study how a family of specific Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) could substantially decrease the false-positive ratio, without asymptotic increase of SRC-search time and storage, compared to the classical 1D-Tree. We perform a competitive analysis of a $c$-DAG with respect to the 1D-Tree and derive only an {\bf\em additive constant Returned Level Overhead} while reaching a substantial {\bf\em multiplicative logarithmic improvement in the Accuracy Ratio}, on average. We also provide a generic framework extending our results to non-uniform datasets whose level overhead distribution is close to that of a uniform dataset. We define and analyze several single-path local selection rules that can substantially speed up the original SRC-search algorithm, which was based on exhaustive search, and their privacy implications. Experiments on the Gowalla and NYC Yellow Taxi datasets show that the level overhead stays at or below the proven constant, up to sampling error, and that the level overhead distribution of real data is close to a uniform baseline in most configurations.
item.dc:creator: Ladan Kian, Dariusz R. Kowalski

item.title: A Better Analysis For PPSZ For 3-SAT
item.description: arXiv:2607.10697v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The PPSZ algorithm of Paturi, Pudl\'ak, Saks, and Zane solves 3-SAT by processing the variables in a uniformly random order, setting a variable whenever a bounded number of clauses implies its value, and guessing it otherwise. Its running time is determined by how many variables are forced in this process, and the exact exponent is a central question in the study of exponential-time satisfiability algorithms. Scheder showed that the classical analysis of PPSZ is not tight for 3-SAT. We ask how much further a sharper analysis of the unmodified algorithm can go. Our analysis uses auxiliary distributions on variable orderings that correlate the positions of variables sharing critical clauses. Such correlations make forcing more likely for some variables, can make it less likely for others, and incur an entropy cost. We choose the correlated pairs at random on short components, so that every pair is selected with the same probability, and we express the forcing loss as a sum of weights attached to these pairs in advance. Gains and losses then scale by the same factor and can be compared directly. Combining the resulting estimate with the complementary estimate of Scheder through an explicit linear-programming certificate gives a uniform improvement for every uniquely satisfiable formula. We prove that the original PPSZ algorithm, with a sufficiently large but fixed implication strength, solves Unique-3-SAT in randomized time $O^*(1.306969598^n)$. Through the lifting framework of Scheder and Steinberger, it solves general 3-SAT in randomized time $O^*(1.307031578^n)$. Both bounds improve the guarantees obtained from the analysis of Scheder for the same algorithm. These improvements follow entirely from the analysis, while PPSZ continues to use a uniformly random variable order and unbiased guesses. It shows that the known guarantees for PPSZ can be strengthened by analysis alone.
item.dc:creator: Tao Jiang, Shaowei Cai

item.title: Online Service with Per-Batch Maximum Delays
item.description: arXiv:2608.18577v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study online service with per-batch maximum delays on a finite metric space. Requests arrive over time, and a server serves each batch by following a walk visiting its requests' locations. Movement is instantaneous. The objective is to minimize the total distance traveled by the server plus the sum, over all batches, of the maximum waiting time in each batch. We give deterministic polynomial-time algorithms with competitive ratios $10$ on finite lines, $12$ on weighted trees, and $20$ on arbitrary finite metrics. Unlike additive delay, maximum delay allows younger requests to join a batch without increasing its delay charge. Our algorithms coordinate service using a common waiting clock and a threshold determined by the metric. The analysis uses certificates for groups of requests to compare this policy with any offline schedule, even one that serves different batches and follows different walks. This comparison shows that coordinating service in this way loses only a constant factor. The bounds hold whether the server must serve requests it visits or may leave them unserved; the two rules also have equal offline optimal costs. Offline optimization is polynomial on lines and explicitly represented weighted trees, and NP hard on general metrics. When arrivals are announced but locations are hidden until visited, we give an $84$-competitive algorithm on a known finite line under either rule.
item.dc:creator: Tianhang Lu, Runtian Ren, Shengcai Liu, Ke Tang

item.title: A Faster Auction Algorithm for Weighted Matroid Intersection
item.description: arXiv:2610.00920v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider the weighted matroid intersection problem in the independence-oracle model. A sequence of works by Huang--Kakimura--Kamiyama~[SODA'16 \& Math. Program'19], Chekuri--Quanrud~[SODA'16], Quanrud~[ICALP'24], and Dudeja--Grilnberger~[IPCO'26] has developed efficient $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithms for this problem. We present a simple deterministic auction algorithm that, given two matroids on a common ground set of size $n$, computes a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate maximum-weight common independent set using $O(n \varepsilon^{-2} \log^2(n))$ independence-oracle queries. This is the first deterministic $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for the weighted matroid intersection problem whose query complexity is nearly linear in $n$ and polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$. Our algorithm builds on the auction algorithm for unweighted matroid intersection by Huang--Kobayashi~['26].
item.dc:creator: Tatsuya Terao

item.title: Power of Conditional Sampling on Hypergraphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.23364v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a $d$-uniform hypergraph with $|V|=n$ and $|E|=m$. Estimating $m$ from uniformly random hyperedge samples requires $\Theta(\sqrt{m})$ samples by a birthday-paradox argument. We investigate the power of conditional sampling through a hierarchy of oracles: for an integer $1\le s\le d$, given pairwise disjoint subsets $X_1,\ldots,X_s\subseteq V$, the $s$-colorful oracle returns a hyperedge chosen uniformly at random from all hyperedges contained in $X_1\cup\cdots\cup X_s$ that intersect every $X_i$, provided one exists. For $s=1$, this samples a uniformly random hyperedge induced by $X_1$. For every $1\le s\le d$, we give a randomized algorithm that outputs $\widehat{m}\in[(1-\varepsilon)m,(1+\varepsilon)m]$ with probability at least $2/3$ using $O_{s,d}(\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon,\log n))$ conditional samples, where the exponent of $\log n$ is an absolute constant independent of both $s$ and $d$. Conditional sampling thus yields an exponential separation over uniform hyperedge sampling. We also study the decision version, in which the oracle only reports whether a qualifying hyperedge exists. For every $1\le s<d$, we prove that any algorithm using the $s$-colorful decision oracle requires $\widetilde{\Omega}_{s,d}(n^{\frac{d-s}{d-s+1}})$ queries. Hence, for $s<d$, access to uniformly random witness hyperedges (random certificates) is exponentially more powerful than existence queries. For $s=d$, decision queries alone achieve $\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon,\log n)$ query complexity, but the exponent of $\log n$ is known to be $\Theta(d)$. The colorful hierarchy thus exhibits a phase transition at $s=d$: for $s<d$, random certificates are essential for polylogarithmic-query estimation, whereas at $s=d$ decision queries suffice, yet random certificates still provably reduce the exponent of $\log n$ from $\Theta(d)$ to an absolute constant.
item.dc:creator: Debarshi Chanda, Buddha Dev Das, Arijit Ghosh, Gopinath Mishra

item.title: Amplified Pruning and Path Selectors for Deterministic Radio Gossiping
item.description: arXiv:2610.28930v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study deterministic gossiping in unknown strongly connected directed radio networks with $n$ vertices, $m$ arcs, and distinct identifiers in $[N]$, where $N=n^{\mathcal O(1)}$. Messages are unrestricted and collision detection is unavailable. Our neighborhood-clearing procedure reuses an elected receiver to secure its entire closed in-neighborhood in $\mathcal O(n\log^2n\log\log n)$ rounds. Charging each distinct closed neighborhood once yields $\mathcal O(m\log^2n\log\log n)$ rounds under an explicit degree-concentration condition, for every polynomial identifier range. A complementary adaptive-pruning procedure combines quadratic contraction with completion sensitive to the number of unsecured sources. If $a\ge1$ sources remain at completion entry, permutation selectors reduce the balanced completion budget by a factor of $\log^{2/3}(a+1)$ relative to interleaved path selectors. A geometric execution attains $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(k^2+n\tau+\min\{u^2,(nu)^{2/3}\})$ for a path cover of scale $k$, weight $\tau$, and $u$ exceptions. For directed graphs with common in- and out-degree $\Delta$, the portfolio achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n\sqrt\Delta,n^2/\Delta\})$. Every graph also admits $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n^{4/3},N+(mn)^{3/5}\})$ rounds. Only $n,N$ are inputs; degrees, covers, and structural constants are used solely in the analysis. The unrestricted polynomial-identifier density extension remains open.
item.dc:creator: Qin Xin

item.title: A Tight Space Lower Bound for Pivot-Based Distance Oracles
item.description: arXiv:2610.29624v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An approximate distance oracle (ADO) is a compact data structure that answers distance queries within a multiplicative \emph{stretch} $k$. The classical oracle of Thorup and Zwick~[STOC'01, JACM'05] has stretch $k=2\ell-1$ and uses $O(\ell n^{1+1/\ell})$ space, for every integer $\ell\ge1$, and this trade-off is optimal for dense graphs under the Erd\H{o}s girth conjecture. However, for sparse graphs ($m=O(n)$), their lower bound yields nothing beyond $\Omega(m)$ space. A pivot-based $1$-hop ADO gives every vertex $\tilde{O}(1)$ pivots and returns as an estimate the length of a walk of the form $u\to p_u \to p_v \to v$, where $p_u$ is a pivot of $u$, $p_v$ is a pivot of $v$, and $p_u\to p_v$ is a stored distance. We observe that all the state-of-the-art ADOs with $\tilde{O}(1)$ query time are in fact pivot-based $1$-hop ADOs. Our main result is that, under the Erd\H{o}s girth conjecture for graphs with constant degree, there are sparse graphs on which every \emph{pivot-based} $1$-hop ADO with stretch $k$ requires $\widetilde\Omega(m^{1+2/(k+1)})$ space, for every \emph{real} $k\ge1$. This matches the best known upper bounds with $\tilde{O}(1)$ query time, up to polylogarithmic factors, at every stretch where they are known. We also extend our lower bound to pivot-based ADOs with any constant number $\beta$ of hops, showing that they require $\widetilde\Omega(m^{1+2/(\beta(k+1))})$ space. In addition, we obtain a tight lower bound for two-hop hopsets. Under the Erd\H{o}s girth conjecture, for every integer $\ell\ge3$, $(2\ell-3,2)$-hopsets on sparse graphs require size $\Omega(m^{1+1/\ell})$, which matches a construction based on the oracles of [Kadria and Roditty, ISAAC'25]. Using the recent explicit high-girth graphs of Double Agent~[doubleAI'26], we also obtain unconditional versions of our ADO lower bounds, with the exponent above $1$ multiplied by $4/5$.
item.dc:creator: Avi Kadria, Liam Roditty

item.title: Exact Algorithms and Complexity of the Smallest Grammar Problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.32298v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Smallest Grammar Problem (SGP) asks for a smallest straight-line grammar generating a given string, with size measured by the total right-hand-side length. For an input of length $n\ge2$ over at most $\sigma$ symbols, where $2\le\sigma\le n$, let $R=\log_\sigma n$. We give a deterministic exact algorithm running in $n^{O(1)}2^{O(n\log\log n/(R\sqrt{\log n}))}$ time and polynomial space, with constants independent of $\sigma$. This gives time $2^{O(n\log\log n/(\log n)^{3/2})}$ for fixed alphabets and $2^{O(n\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n})}$ for arbitrary alphabets, up to polynomial factors. The algorithm combines pairwise disjoint representative occurrences of dictionary strings, a sparse interval certificate, and the Boolean tensor contraction theorem of OpenAI. It explicitly enforces dictionary membership, rule boundaries, and the grammar-size budget. Independently of that contraction theorem, disjoint representatives yield exact algorithms in $O^*(1.872258^n)$ time and $2^{O((n/R)\log(R+1))}$ time using $O(n)$ words of space. Anchor-based grammar projections establish binary NP-completeness and reductions with tunable alphabet size. We state their consequences as unconditional quantitative transfers from SGP algorithms to sparse SAT algorithms, and quantify the additional loss from sparsifying general formulas.
item.dc:creator: Xiangle Chen

item.title: A Search-Based Algorithm for Multistage Robust Discrete Linear Optimization and its Implementation
item.description: arXiv:2210.11132v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robust optimization models that allow decisions to adapt to newly revealed information remain computationally challenging and are often limited to two decision stages or are addressed heuristically or via approximation schemes. This challenge is further amplified when uncertainty sets depend on earlier decisions. Conventional approaches to such problems often require problem-specific reformulations and tailored algorithms, highlighting the need for an exact model-and-run approach. We address this gap by presenting an algorithmic framework for solving multistage robust discrete linear optimization problems. This exact approach adapts and integrates ideas from game-tree search, quantified conflict-driven clause learning, and integer linear programming to explore the minimax tree and is implemented in the open-source solver Yasol. The solver supports discrete decision variables across multiple stages, discrete uncertainty sets with polyhedral or decision-dependent structure, and mixed-integer recourse in the final stage. It can be used as a standalone executable or through a C++ library interface, allowing it to serve as a reference solver for exact methods in multistage robust discrete linear optimization. In an extensive computational study, we demonstrate the capabilities of our solver. The results show competitive performance against a reference approach from the literature for a protection-interdiction problem, as well as strong performance on bilevel benchmark instances. For a multistage cutting-stock problem, we demonstrate the substantial loss in solution quality that can arise from neglecting the multistage structure and show that our solver significantly outperforms decision-rule approximations in terms of computational efficiency while certifying the true multistage optimum.
item.dc:creator: Michael Hartisch, Ulf Lorenz

item.title: Nash Incentive-compatible Online Mechanism Learning via Weakly Differentially Private Online Learning
item.description: arXiv:2407.04898v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study a multi-round mechanism design problem, where we interact with a set of agents over a sequence of rounds. We wish to design an incentive-compatible (IC) online learning scheme to maximize an application-specific objective within a given class of mechanisms, without prior knowledge of the agents' type distributions. Even if each mechanism in this class is IC in a single round, if an algorithm naively chooses from this class on each round, the entire learning process may not be IC against non-myopic buyers who appear over multiple rounds. On each round, our method randomly chooses between the recommendation of a weakly differentially private online learning algorithm (e.g., Hedge), and a commitment mechanism which penalizes non-truthful behavior. Our method is IC and achieves $O(T^{\frac{1+h}{2}})$ regret for the application-specific objective in an adversarial setting, where $h$ quantifies the long-sightedness of the agents. When compared to prior work, our approach is conceptually simpler,it applies to general mechanism design problems (beyond auctions), and its regret scales gracefully with the size of the mechanism class.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235:20643-20659, 2024
item.dc:creator: Joon Suk Huh, Kirthevasan Kandasamy

item.title: Polynomial and Hyperplane Avoidance over the Integers with Applications to Integer-Point Counting
item.description: arXiv:2411.07030v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the \emph{Polynomial Avoidance Problem}: given a finite collection $F \subseteq Z[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ of nonzero polynomials, find a vector $x \in Z^n$ of minimum $\ell_p$-norm such that $f(x)\neq0$ for every $f \in F$. Each polynomial is given sparsely as a list of its nonzero terms. The affine special case is the \emph{Hyperplane Avoidance Problem}. This special case arises in Barvinok-type algorithms for counting integer points in polyhedra, when certain rational generating functions must be evaluated at a removable singularity. Our main results are as follows: 1) Let $D:=\sum_{f\in F} \text{deg} f$. Every instance admits a feasible vector $x$ satisfying \[ \|x\|_1 \leq \min\left\{D,\frac{D+n}{2}\right\}. \] This bound is tight. Such a vector can be found by a deterministic algorithm whose bit complexity is polynomial in $D$ and the sparse encoding length of the input. Our proof uses a new algorithmic variant of the \emph{Combinatorial Nullstellensatz}; 2) In the affine case, with $m$ input polynomials, such a vector can be constructed by a fast deterministic polynomial-time algorithm using $O(nm)$ arithmetic operations. For the homogeneous case, Barvinok's original approach provides only the weaker guarantee $\|x\|_1 = O((nm)^{n-1})$; 3) The problem is NP-hard for every $p\in R_{\geq 1}\cup\{\infty\}$, even for homogeneous linear forms; 4) As an application, we improve the complexity bound for counting integer points in general rational polytopes. We also improve the bound for polyhedra of bounded codimension; this includes the counting version of the \emph{Unbounded Subset-Sum} problem as a special case.
item.dc:creator: Grigorii Dakhno, Dmitry Gribanov, Nikita Kasianov, Anastasiia Kats, Andrey Kupavskii, Nikita Kuz'min, Stanislav Moiseev

item.title: An Unconditional Lower Bound for the Active-Set Method in Almost-Linear Programming
item.description: arXiv:2507.16648v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove that, for every fixed $\epsilon\in(0,1]$, the active-set method requires exponentially many iterations in the worst case to maximize a convex objective of the form $(x_1)^{1+\epsilon}+\vec c^{\top}\vec x$ subject to linear constraints, regardless of the pivot rule used. Our lower bound therefore holds for objectives arbitrarily close to the linear case $\epsilon=0$, where the active-set method coincides with the simplex method and a lower bound for all pivot rules would constitute a major breakthrough. The special case $\epsilon=1$ yields a lower bound in convex quadratic maximization. This improves on the best previously known lower bound [IPCO 2025] requiring polynomial objectives of degree $\omega(\log d)$ in dimension $d$ and firmly resolves the open question of whether a constant degree suffices. Our result is based on a novel extended formulation, recursively constructed using deformed products. Its key feature is that it projects onto a polygonal approximation of a parabola while preserving all of its exponentially many vertices. We define a convex objective with a single non-linear variable that forces the active-set method to follow the parabolic boundary of this projection, without allowing any shortcuts along chords corresponding to edges of its full-dimensional preimage.
item.dc:creator: Eleon Bach, Yann Disser, Sophie Huiberts, Nils Mosis

item.title: Approximate Envy-Freeness and Pareto Optimality Beyond Additivity
item.description: arXiv:2607.18220v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the compatibility of envy-freeness up to one good (EF1) and Pareto optimality (PO) beyond additive valuations. For two agents with monotone submodular valuations, we prove that a $2/3$-EF1+PO allocation always exists, while for every $\alpha>3/4$, an $\alpha$-EF1+PO allocation may fail to exist even for unweighted coverage valuations. A six-good EF1+PO counterexample resolves the longstanding exact existence question negatively. Exact EF1+PO does exist when one agent has a monotone submodular valuation and the remaining agents have identical additive valuations. For two agents, we also establish tight EF$k$+PO item thresholds of $4k+1$, $2k+1$, and $3k+1$ for two submodular agents, two subadditive agents, and one subadditive and one additive agent, respectively. Finally, deciding whether an EF$k$+PO allocation exists is NP-hard for every fixed integer $k\ge1$, even for three agents with unweighted coverage valuations, one of whom has an additive valuation.
item.dc:creator: Harish Chandramouleeswaran, Prajakta Nimbhorkar

item.title: Improved Lower Bounds on Tree Covers
item.description: arXiv:2607.27264v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A tree cover of an $n$-point metric space is a collection of $k$ trees such that every pairwise distance is approximately preserved in at least one tree. For fixed $k$, the best known distortion upper bound is $\tilde{O}(n^{1/k})$ and the best known lower bound is $\Omega_k(n^{1/2^{k-1}})$. In this paper, we prove a lower bound of $\Omega_k(n^{1/(k-1)^2})$ for all $k\ge 3$, significantly narrowing the gap towards the upper bound. Our approach makes use of a novel algebraic topological notion that we call the \emph{agreement index}: the equivariant topological index of a simplicial complex encoding pairwise agreement among tree labels. This notion helps characterize the power and limit of algebraic and topological methods for analyzing tree covers, and we believe it will also find applications to other problems.
item.dc:creator: Yu Chen, Shengtang Huang, Zihan Tan, Hangyu Xu

item.title: GPU-Accelerated Search for Fast Matrix Multiplication over $\mathbb{F}_2$
item.description: arXiv:2609.17533v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a GPU-accelerated algorithm for searching for ways to multiply matrices with few scalar multiplications. Our algorithm searches the matrix multiplication flip graph and, on an NVIDIA H200, performs over a billion search steps per second for matrix sizes up to $7\times7$, a roughly $380\times$ improvement over previous GPU-accelerated search on the tensor for $7\times7$ matrix multiplication. We also prove that, over \(\mathbb{F}_2\), the directed matrix multiplication flip graph is strongly connected with only flip and plus edges. This removes the need for computationally expensive reduction edges in the connectivity argument used by previous work. Using this GPU-accelerated search procedure on our simplified flip graph, we find a way to multiply $7\times 7$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2$ using 245 multiplications, a three-multiplication improvement over the previous record.
item.dc:creator: Zeke Medley, Anagha Gokul, Quan Luu, Panagiotis Manolios

item.title: Report the tolerance, not the count: exact phylogenetic distance deconvolution with incomplete references
item.description: arXiv:2610.30776v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Phylogenetic distance deconvolution represents mixture-to-reference distances by weighted sources placed on a reference tree. We study the minimum number of strictly interior sources that explains a distance profile, and what incomplete references cost. On a positive-rational reduced tree we give an exact algorithm with 2^O(K) poly(B) bit complexity for a free positive mean pendant and any nonempty set of observed leaves; the single-exponential dependence on K is tight under ETH, already with every leaf observed. With arbitrary missing references and a prescribed pendant the problem is W[1]-hard in the source budget K, even on positive binary trees supplied with a strict explanation using at most K+1 sources. We then use the algorithm as an instrument. Removing references can only lower the minimum source count, never raise it, at every error tolerance. Which references are missing then matters far more than how many. Under nearest-to-source deletion a median of two references can be erased before the generating support stops being the unique smallest explanation, and that budget stays nearly flat as the panel grows (Spearman 0.10 over 20 to 361 references, against 0.82 for random loss). Discarding 7,931 of 10,575 references from a real 16S panel at random costs 1.8% of the tolerance at which one source suffices. Discarding comparably many as whole clades costs 90%. That tolerance needs neither ground truth nor an error model, which makes the model measurable on real data. The generating configuration's worst-leaf residual exceeds the one-source optimum in all 296 real ANI cases, and in 248 after refitting the common pendant. The phenomenon is not unobservable in practice. A point estimate of the count alone does not quantify it. Methods for this problem should report the tolerance at which an explanation of a given size exists.
